title: India's 7.8% Growth Beats Forecasts — But Few Indians Feel It
excerpt: The June-quarter print smashed expectations, yet economists and critics question the numbers and point to weak jobs, uneven consumption and a fight over the data methodology.
body:
• India's economy grew 7.8% in the June quarter (Q1 FY27), beating the 7.1% forecast in a Reuters poll, on an investment boom and manufacturing strength.
  • The pace was down from an upward-revised 8.6% in the previous quarter, and economists flagged red flags beneath the headline: inflation, uneven monsoons and geopolitical risk.
  • Former finance secretary Subhash Chandra Garg claimed true growth was closer to 2.6%, arguing a downward revision of the year-ago base flattered the number; the statistics ministry rejected any systematic bias.
  • Former RBI governor Raghuram Rajan asked why strong GDP growth is not showing up in job creation, domestic investment or foreign portfolio inflows.

India's economy grew 7.8% in the June quarter, beating analyst forecasts and handing Prime Minister Narendra Modi a number he hailed as a "Herculean feat" — but the celebration has been drowned out by a noisy debate over whether the headline reflects the economy most Indians actually live in.

Government data showed the world's fifth-biggest economy expanded 7.8% in the three months through June from a year earlier, beating the 7.1% forecast in a Reuters poll, as an investment boom and manufacturing strength added to solid consumer demand. The pace was down from an upward-revised 8.6% in the March quarter, while gross value added growth printed above 8%, according to ICRA chief economist Aditi Nayar. Gross fixed capital formation surged 11.9% — the highest on the current data series — as capital expenditure expanded beyond public balance sheets.

Context & Background

The figures sit on a new 2022-23 GDP series, and India's quarterly estimates are routinely revised as better data arrives — sometimes sharply. Growth for the June quarter of FY26 was first reported at 7.8% in August 2025, revised down to 6.8% in June 2026, then nudged to 6.9% in August 2026. Mint's analysis found India recorded 7%-plus growth in 18 of the 36 years between 1990-91 and 2025-26, but never sustained it: the decadal average never crossed 6.6%. The post-pandemic run of 7%-plus prints has not been enough to offset covid losses — and GDP growth may have decoupled from human welfare as inequality rises and expansion becomes more capital-intensive.

"Herculean feat"

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India, on the 7.8% GDP print

Impact & Analysis

The sharpest challenge came from Subhash Chandra Garg, formerly the finance ministry's top bureaucrat, who argued on September 2 — in a column for The Quint and an interview with NDTV — that real growth was closer to 2.6%. His case: the government had reduced its measure of GDP for the year-earlier quarter, the basis of comparison, making the latest print look stronger.

Raghuram Rajan, the former Reserve Bank of India governor, took a different tack. In a television interview he asked why the robust GDP figure was not showing up in stronger job creation, domestic investment and foreign portfolio inflows — later clarifying on LinkedIn that he had neither questioned nor endorsed the numbers, only asking why strong growth had not translated over time into more private investment, foreign investment and decent jobs.

Statistics secretary Saurabh Garg defended the estimate on the same day, saying the large revisions reflected more granular price signals and additional data sources rather than any systematic bias. The opposition was unconvinced: a top Congress official dismissed the print as "statistical gymnastics."

An economist at IIM Ranchi argued the deeper question is not whether India grew 7.8% — "the data confirm it" — but whether the headline reflects the economy beyond its organised core: gains concentrated in investment-intensive, urban sectors; consumption trailing investment; the informal economy still measured through proxy extrapolation; and a subdued deflator turning 10.3% nominal growth into 7.8% real growth. SBI Capital Markets warned private consumption could face headwinds later in the fiscal year from high prices and muted rural demand. The discontent has a political edge: youth protests prompted the education minister to resign in July, seen as a broader expression of frustration over scarce opportunities and jobs.

What's Next

Economists remain split. L&T Finance chief economist Rajni Thakur called the quarter a "positive surprise" and argued strong capex, robust credit growth and continued policy support should sustain activity above 7% for the fiscal year. But risks crowd the horizon: global uncertainties, El Nino and the West Asia conflict's impact on exposed sectors. Reuters Breakingviews noted the headline figure's credibility has significantly improved — but called for more transparency on inputs to reduce surprises in the $4 trillion economy's data. The next test comes when ordinary Indians start feeling the growth in their paychecks.

nri_angle: The growth-versus-jobs debate shapes the economic reality that diaspora readers' families in India live with.
